title: JPMorgan, Citi and Barclays Are Now on DTCC's Tokenization Rails. Why Is Canton (CC) Still Down 21% This Month? - 24/7 Wall St.
content:
JPMorgan, Citi, Barclays, and 17 other financial giants just signed onto DTCC's blockchain settlement platform, yet the coin powering that network keeps sliding deeper into the red. Something about how these banks actually use the network may surprise CC holders. The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) launched its Tokenization Service on October 28, 2026, a significant step for post-trade operations in the U.S. stock and bond markets. This service enables the creation of blockchain tokens that represent traditional securities, using the Canton Network, which relies on Canton Coin (CRYPTO: CC). To date, 20 participants have signed up to use this service from DTC, the depository arm of the DTCC, including major banks and brokerages that hold securities at DTC. DTC holds over $114 trillion in assets under custody, and the participants include Barclays (NYSE: BCS), Citigroup (NYSE: C | C Price Prediction), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), Morgan Stanley, and State Street (NYSE: STT). The Tokenization Service operates on two networks: the Canton Network and DTCC’s private Besu network, with plans to add more networks in 2027. Despite these advancements, Canton Coin’s value has continued to decline. CC traded at $0.1005, up 1.1% over the past 24 hours but still down 20.4% for the month. This dip is significant, as CC is 48.2% below its all-time high of $0.1942, reached on February 3, 2026. Canton Strategic Holdings (NASDAQ: CNTN) recently divested its legacy biotech division, Gravitas Life Sciences, to focus on Canton-related businesses. As a Super Validator on the Canton Network, the company earns CC rewards. It also offers a Locking-as-a-Service product that secures CC for participants who must maintain minimum balances according to governance rules. In the second quarter of 2026, these operations generated about $1.5 million in revenue, primarily from the new Locking-as-a-Service, which contributed $1.3 million. However, the company reported a net loss of $19 million due to the declining value of its 3.71 billion CC holdings, resulting in a $24 million unrealized loss, which reflects the depreciation of assets still on the books. Looking ahead, the company plans to list tokenized shares on TSV LLC, a blockchain trading platform, with trading expected to start as soon as November 2 under the SEC’s Innovation Exemption. Fairmint’s tokens are designed to carry the same rights as the company’s Nasdaq shares. However, the announcement does not clarify whether buyers will use CC for these transactions, suggesting trades may involve cash tokens or stablecoins, with CC serving only as a fee currency. While DTCC has welcomed 20 banks and brokers to its network, it has not guaranteed they will purchase, hold, or transact in Canton Coin. Institutions can avoid public-token systems entirely by using the Besu network. Their participation signals support for DTCC’s initiatives rather than a direct endorsement of Canton Coin. CC serves as the utility token for the Canton network, enabling applications to pay synchronizer fees—a system that organizes and confirms transactions. CC fees are burned, permanently removing those tokens from circulation. The network mints new tokens as rewards for app providers and validators based on their activity, so the overall CC supply grows as usage increases. However, under governance proposal CIP-0129, traffic on dedicated synchronizers will not contribute to burning CC. DTCC has not specified which type of synchronizer it will use for its Canton transactions, leaving CC holders uncertain. If transactions occur on a dedicated synchronizer, it may generate DTCC fees while saving banks time, but it could also burn less CC. The participating banks are also developing their own systems. Citi’s CEO, Jane Fraser, highlighted on the October 13 earnings call that Citi Token Services and tokenized deposits are key areas of focus, and the bank operates its own competing network connecting 300 banks. State Street CEO Ron O’Hanley said on October 14 that its tokenized fund platform will launch by year-end, with its cash fund operating on Stellar. Meanwhile, JPMorgan has its own tokenized fund offerings. On October 23, Canton’s Super Validators approved CIP-0129, which introduces universal burning: every production synchronizer will burn CC at a specified list price, with volume discounts for high-frequency users. A subsequent proposal is needed to set prices, but for now, the network is minting more CC than it burns. The discounts could mean large users, likely banks, burn less CC per transaction. Additionally, the Canton Development Fund has allocated 15.8 million CC (valued at about $1.6 million) to RedStone to develop CAPS, a privacy-focused pricing standard still in development. If grant recipients sell their CC, it could further exert downward pressure on the token’s price. This ongoing situation is reflected in CC’s performance, which is trading below its 20-day, 50-day, and 200-day moving averages, indicating continued market struggles. title: GT Metabolic Solutions Raises Series C Led By J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital - Pulse 2.0
content: GT Metabolic Solutions has secured a Series C growth investment from J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital to accelerate commercialization of its magnetic anastomosis technology. The financing will support the company’s global commercial launch and expansion into additional surgical and therapeutic applications, including endoscopic and colorectal procedures. GT Metabolic develops a linear magnetic anastomosis system that creates gastrointestinal connections without incisions, sutures, or staples. The technology uses magnetic compression to create anastomoses while avoiding permanent foreign material that could interfere with healing. The system can be used with endoscopic, robotic, or laparoscopic surgical approaches. GT Metabolic said gastrointestinal anastomotic procedures can result in serious complications such as leaks and bleeding, which can lead to sepsis, hospital readmission, and death. The company’s magnetic platform is designed to create seamless connections while preserving natural biology and potentially reducing complication rates. GT Metabolic was the first company to receive both an FDA De Novo grant and 510(k) clearance for magnetic technology used to create compression anastomoses. The J.P. Morgan financing represents the company’s first institutional financing partnership. GT Metabolic plans to use the proceeds for product development, surgeon training, worldwide commercial expansion, and development of additional indications. The company has locations in Minneapolis, San Jose, and Montréal. J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital focuses on early-stage biotechnology and later-stage healthcare companies, including medical devices, pharmaceutical services, biopharma, tools, and diagnostics. The investment represents the fifth transaction completed by the J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital team. “The use of magnets in surgery is a game-changing technology to address serious adverse events, such as leaks and bleeding, which have troubled surgeons since the advent of minimally invasive surgery over 50 years ago.” Joe Siletto, Managing Partner At J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital “J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital’s growth investment will help accelerate both product development, surgeon trainings and worldwide commercial expansion.” Thierry Thaure, Co-Founder And CEO Of GT Metabolic Solutions “We are proud to partner with GT Metabolic as it works to transform minimally invasive surgical care.” Anthony Perry, Vice President At J.P. Targeted controls can help address card-not-present fraud and card testing, while limiting unnecessary declines and protecting revenue and the customer experience. U.S. online holiday spending from November 1 through December 31, 2025, was up 6.8% year over year, according to Adobe Analytics.1 For e-commerce merchants, one of the biggest concerns is card-not-present (CNP) fraud, which involves using payment credentials fraudulently when the physical card isn’t presented. Fraud pressure tends to rise when merchants are busiest. CNP fraud, card testing, chargeback abuse and automated attacks can all increase operational strain at the same time teams are trying to keep checkout moving. More suspected fraudulent activity was blocked by certain card networks globally over the 2025 Black Friday and Cyber Monday weekend than during the same period a year earlier.2 Merchants balance CNP fraud prevention with the customer experience. Controls ideally reduce losses while preserving legitimate approvals, authorization rates and revenue. Peak shopping periods give fraudsters more activity to blend into. A sudden increase in transactions can make unusual behavior harder to isolate, while operations teams have less time to investigate each exception. Card testing is an automated fraud tactic in which stolen or compromised card credentials are tested through low-dollar transactions to determine whether they’re active. Attackers may then use validated credentials for fraudulent purchases.3 CNP fraud can be difficult to distinguish from valid e-commerce activity because the transaction itself may look ordinary. High holiday volumes can also make automated attacks harder to isolate. That makes transaction context increasingly important. Customer, payment and transaction patterns can help merchants identify activity that may warrant additional review. Fraud during peak shopping periods can take several forms. Merchants may see compromised cards used for online purchases, bursts of low-value card-testing attempts or dispute abuse that surfaces after an order has been fulfilled. AI can make fraudulent activity easier to automate and scale. During peak shopping periods, higher volumes can make that activity harder to distinguish from normal customer behavior.4 That puts more pressure on merchants to identify risk without adding unnecessary friction for legitimate customers. The financial impact can extend well beyond the original purchase. The FBI reports that credit card fraud accounted for $282 million in losses in 2025, while non-payment and non-delivery scams resulted in more than $503 million in losses.5 The agency also notes that complaint volume often rises in the early months of the year, suggesting a connection to holiday-season scams. Tightening controls across the board may help protect against some fraud, but it can also create unnecessary friction for customers. Overly restrictive controls can create false declines—where legitimate transactions are rejected as suspicious—and reduce authorization rates, the share of transactions approved.6 During the holidays, that added friction comes at a particularly important point in the customer journey. A more targeted approach applies additional scrutiny where risk is higher, while allowing lower-risk activity to move with less interruption. Using multiple checks can support that balance by bringing together different signals rather than relying on a single rule or threshold.7 Merchants can also adjust controls as behavior changes throughout the season. A pattern that looks unusual in October may be completely normal during a major shopping weekend. That balance can help merchants respond to changing fraud patterns without adding unnecessary friction at checkout. Chargebacks can create work long after the original purchase. Teams may need to investigate disputes, gather documentation and respond within network timelines, adding costs that can affect the bottom line. Card-testing attacks can create additional processing costs and may also lead to payment network monitoring, chargebacks and potential fines.8 False declines create a different kind of loss. A shopper whose purchase is incorrectly declined may abandon it entirely, reducing revenue and potentially weakening the customer relationship. There’s also a broader confidence issue. Customers expect payment experiences to feel both secure and easy. Fraud controls that add checkout steps or delays can work against that experience, while streamlined payments can support customer loyalty.9 That’s why fraud performance should be considered alongside authorization rates, dispute levels and customer experience. Looking across fraud losses, false declines, chargebacks, conversion and review workload can give merchants a fuller picture of how their controls are performing. Preparation starts before transaction volumes rise. Merchants can focus on a few areas as peak season approaches: Technology plays an important role, but the surrounding processes matter just as much. Fraud tools should support secure, compliant payment experiences while giving teams enough visibility to understand why activity is being flagged and how controls are performing. Card-not-present fraud occurs when stolen or compromised payment credentials are used without the physical card being presented, commonly in e-commerce or other remote transactions. Card testing uses small, repeated authorization attempts to determine whether stolen card credentials are still active. Successful credentials may then be used for larger fraudulent purchases. Risk-based controls can apply more scrutiny to higher-risk activity while allowing lower-risk transactions to move with less friction. Monitoring performance across fraud losses, false declines and authorization rates can help merchants understand whether controls are working as intended. Useful measures include fraud loss, false-decline rates, authorization or approval rates, chargeback rates, conversion and manual-review workload. Looking at those measures together gives a more complete picture than relying on one metric alone. Holiday shopping creates a narrow window in which merchants need to move quickly without losing control of risk. The strongest fraud strategies are built around that balance: identifying high-risk activity early while keeping valid customers moving. That requires monitoring, adaptable controls and a clear view of how fraud decisions affect approvals, disputes and customer experience. Fraud tactics will continue to evolve. Preparing early and adapting controls as patterns change can help merchants respond without adding unnecessary checkout friction or losing sight of customer trust and growth. title: When Markets Feel Like a Bubble: What Should Investors Do? - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
The Private Bank’s mission is to build, preserve & transform our client’s wealth. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The word "bubble" is everywhere again. Three centuries ago, Sir Isaac Newton — one of the greatest minds who ever lived — was an early investor in the South Sea Company. He rode the shares up, sold, and pocketed a handsome profit. But as the stock kept climbing and those around him grew rich, he bought back in near the peak with a large share of his wealth and lost it all. His verdict, as it is often recounted, has echoed ever since: "I can calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people." Three hundred years later, we understand Newton’s law of gravity a little better, but nothing else has changed. In early 2021, a single stock — GameStop — rocketed from around ＄20 to more than＄450 in a matter of weeks,1 propelled not by earnings but by social media and the sight of others getting rich fast. This is FOMO — the fear of missing out — in its purest financial form: the anxiety of watching others profit becomes stronger than the discipline to stay grounded in fundamentals. Many piled in near the top; when it collapsed just as quickly, they were left holding the losses. Different eras, different assets, same story. Whenever markets rise sharply around a powerful investment theme, the same question returns: how far is too far? Headlines turn increasingly cautious; investors begin questioning whether prices have outrun fundamentals, and the temptation grows to step aside before the inevitable correction. That anxiety is not irrational. Throughout history, there have been periods when prices became difficult to justify against underlying fundamentals. Some ended in painful corrections; others took years to unwind. This piece takes no view on whether today's market is one of them — that call is notoriously unreliable in real time, even for professionals. That said, in our view, regardless of whether current market optimism does or does not prove to be a bubble, we believe there remains genuine value in the AI (artificial intelligence) thesis and opportunities to continue benefiting from the trend. The more useful question, and the one we focus on here, is how to stay exposed to that opportunity while managing the risks that come with it. And to manage those risks well, it helps to understand what a bubble actually is — how it forms, and why it has caught even the most brilliant investors for centuries. A bubble, in essence, occurs when asset prices become hard to justify by fundamentals and depend increasingly on the belief that someone else will pay more later. Most follow a recognizable progression: a genuine opportunity emerges, prices rise, success stories draw in more capital, momentum reinforces belief, and valuations stretch — until new buyers become essential to sustaining prices, the flow of new money slows, and the cycle reverses. Financial history is full of episodes that looked different on the surface but shared familiar characteristics. Railways did transform commerce. The internet did change the global economy. Housing is a vital economic asset. Japan really was an extraordinary success before its late-1980s boom. But a genuine opportunity says nothing about whether the price being paid for it is reasonable — and that distinction is one of the most important lessons in financial history: "Is the opportunity real?" and "Is it attractively priced?" are different questions. Every bubble looks different. The behavioral pattern does not. The progression above has repeated for four centuries; only the asset and the story change. But each episode also leaves behind a distinct lesson. The common thread is humbling: knowing a bubble may exist tells you little about when it will burst, how far it will run first, or what the right response is. That uncertainty — not the bubble itself — is the real problem to solve. And because you can be right about the long run yet still be forced to sell at the worst possible moment, being early can cost as much as being wrong. Even the most experienced and sophisticated investors participate in bubbles. And for understandable reasons, according to behavioral science. Intelligence does not immunize investors against behavior. Once an investment becomes something discussed with colleagues, friends, the media — and increasingly people who don't normally invest — the price itself becomes part of the story. So bubbles are not simply periods of irrationality; they are periods in which reasonable beliefs are amplified by momentum, social reinforcement, and extrapolation. And momentum can persist far longer than logic suggests — the hard truth behind the market adage, often attributed to John Maynard Keynes, that "the market can remain irrational longer than you can stay solvent." Being right about a bubble is not the same as being able to profit from it. Suppose you are convinced the market has run too far. Valuation is only one sign of a stretched market — sentiment, leverage, and a rush of new issuance often say more — but it is the one investors reach for first, and the one that most often misleads them. Because the uncomfortable truth is that conviction alone doesn't help you: acting on it is far harder than it looks. Investors often treat an all-time high as evidence that markets have become too expensive. Psychologically this makes sense — buying after a long rise feels less comfortable than buying after a fall. But the historical data do not support the idea that a record high is, on its own, a reason to wait. The investor who keeps holding out for a better entry may get the pullback they want — or may only get it after the market has climbed substantially higher first. And getting out is only half the decision. Even an investor who correctly senses that valuations are stretched faces a harder second question: not just when to get out, but when to get back in. Selling to cash feels safe while markets fall — but the market never rings a bell to signal the danger has passed, and recoveries often begin while the data still look poor, earnings are under pressure, and the headlines are bleak. Volatility, in other words, is not a bug in the market — it is a feature. It is the very mechanism through which markets reprice risk, reward patient capital, and ultimately deliver the long-term returns that disciplined investors are compensated for enduring. A recovery can begin while economic data still look poor, earnings remain under pressure, and headlines remain negative — which is precisely why the investor waiting for an "all clear" so often misses it. It is worth testing the fear directly. Imagine three investors, each putting the same ＄1,000 to work on seven separate occasions between 1990 and 2022 — ＄7,000 in total. The first has impossibly bad luck. Every single one of her seven investments lands at a market peak, immediately before a major global downturn: just before Japan's bubble burst in 1990, before the Russian debt default and LTCM collapse in 1998, before the dot-com crash in 2000, before the Global Financial Crisis in 2007, before the late-2018 selloff, before the COVID crash in February 2020, and before the 2022 inflation shock. Call her the Unluckiest Investor — she could not have chosen worse moments. The second has perfect foresight, buying instead at the exact low of each of those same downturns — the Luckiest Investor. The third avoids the stress of markets altogether, investing the same amounts on the same dates as the Unluckiest Investor but holding cash (short-term Treasury bills) throughout. By the end of August 2026, the results are striking. Each investor had contributed the same ＄7,000. Perfect timing, of course, won: the Luckiest Investor's stake grew to about ＄39,024 — roughly 5.6× the amount invested. But the part that matters is what happened to the worst-timed investor of all. The Unluckiest Investor — who bought at every single peak, before every single crash — still ended with roughly ＄25,207, or about 3.6× her contributions. The investor who played it "safe" in cash? Just ＄10,881 — barely 1.6×, and less than half of what even the worst-timed equity investor achieved. The lesson is not that timing doesn't matter — clearly, buying low beats buying high. It is that being invested mattered far more than timing it well. The Unluckiest Investor was wrong about the timing every time, and still came out well ahead, because she stayed in the market and let time do the work. The Cash Investor avoided every drawdown — and paid for that comfort with the poorest outcome of all. The implication is not complacency; it is disciplined. A long-term investor does not need to predict peaks to succeed. Even the worst imaginable entry points were overcome simply by staying invested over a long enough horizon. The more durable response to a possible bubble is not to predict risk but to manage it — through three habits that sound simple but are quietly hard to hold: don't retreat to cash out of fear, stay invested, and diversify deliberately. The first two we have already seen: cash quietly erodes purchasing power, and staying invested beat sitting in cash in every scenario above. The third — "diversify" — is the one most often repeated and least understood. Diversification" has become one of the most overused words in investing — nodded along to, rarely defined. In practice it means something different for almost everyone, depending on their goals, their wealth, their career, and their stage of life. For a young saver, it means not betting everything on the one theme that happens to be soaring. For a business owner whose fortune is tied up in one company, it means building income outside that business. For a senior executive, it means making sure the portfolio doesn't simply mirror the industry that already pays their salary. The word is the same; what it requires is not. That is where goals-based planning gives the word real meaning. Rather than "diversified" as a vague virtue, it asks what each pot of money is actually for — and the answer points in different directions. And here is the part almost no one accepts: if you are truly diversified, something you own will always be lagging — if everything rises together, you never were. Tolerating that laggard is the price of protection, and nowhere is it harder than in a bubble, when everything outside the hot theme looks foolish precisely when abandoning the discipline is most tempting. Diversification, properly understood, is about more than what you own — it's about where your wealth comes from. When your salary, your company equity, and your portfolio all ride the same theme — especially the one the market has bid up — a correction hits your income, your net worth, and your investments at once. A portfolio full of different stocks can look diversified on paper while remaining exposed to the very theme everyone is worried about. If your livelihood is already a bet on a theme, your portfolio's job is to be the ballast — not to double down. For many, this is the real question — not "is the market a bubble?" but "what do I do about the large position I already hold in the thing everyone is worried about?" You don't need a view on the bubble to answer it — only on one thing: is this position a larger share of your future than you would ever deliberately choose? Concentration that arrived by accident, from a holding that simply grew, is very different from one you would build today. Most people, asked whether they'd put that share of their net worth into a single position from scratch, would say no — and that gap is what to manage. It need not mean a dramatic exit: you can trim toward the weight you'd actually choose, redirect new capital rather than sell into a tax bill, and — the one hard line — never hold a concentrated position on leverage, which is how being right about the long run still ends in being forced to sell at the worst possible moment. None of this requires predicting the burst. It simply ensures that if a correction comes, it lands on a position sized to your plan — not one large enough to derail it. The tax, liquidity, and timing questions are exactly the conversation to have with your advisor. Notice what all of this has in common: not a single step required knowing whether today's market is a bubble. That is the quiet power of goals-based planning. By dividing wealth into distinct buckets — liquidity, lifestyle, legacy, and perpetual growth — each with its own purpose and time horizon, it turns behavior to your advantage: When each bucket of wealth has its own mission, something quiet powerful happens: the volatility of the long-term assets stops feeling like a threat to the near-term ones. The money you need soon is protected; the money meant to grow is free to do what growth assets do — fluctuate on its way to compounding. And staying the course becomes far easier, because you are no longer asking the market to behave. So the useful question was never "Will the bubble burst?" or "Can I get out in time?" The real question — the one worth answering — is this: "What does each part of this portfolio need to achieve, and is it built to get there through whatever the market does?" Bubbles will keep forming — human nature guarantees it — and what separates the investors who endure is not a sharper ability to call the top, but a plan robust enough that they never have to. title: Alpaca, Citi, JP Morgan among early adopters as DTCC Tokenization Service goes live - Ledger Insights
content: Today the DTCC launched its Tokenization Service after the SEC granted a no-action letter in December 2025. At launch just 34 securities are eligible, a mix of equities, Treasuries and ETFs. The SEC’s no-action letter covers a far broader set, the full Russell 1000, US Treasuries and major index ETFs, worth roughly $30 trillion of the more than $114 trillion DTC holds in custody. These are tokenized entitlements that carry the same ownership rights as conventional securities held in street name at DTC and share the same CUSIP. A key goal is 24/7 transfers. When a tokenized position moves between registered wallets, that is the settlement, so there is no T+1 wait. However, there are limits in the early period. Moving a token between chains goes through DTC’s conversion service, which runs from 2am to 6pm ET on business days, so round the clock transfers are intrachain only. The same service converts positions between conventional and tokenized form. Transfers can only be made between registered wallets. DTC Participants can register selected third party wallets for their clients via a user interface. Twenty DTC Participants have signed up so far. They include global banks and custodians such as JP Morgan, Citi, Bank of America, Barclays, BNP Paribas, UBS, Morgan Stanley and State Street, retail and clearing brokers including Fidelity, Edward Jones, Apex, DriveWealth and Clear Street, and crypto adjacent firms Alpaca and Velocity Capital. Notable absences are BNY, the largest custodian, and Goldman Sachs, which took part in the July live trials. Future users will be onboarded on a rolling basis. There’s a misconception that tokenization is only happening on the Canton Network. DTC’s Besu-based private distributed ledger is also available at launch and provides the foundation for the DTCC Collateral AppChain due early next year. By then additional networks such as Stellar and Circle’s Arc are expected to join the fray, as well as other blockchains subject to client demand. The roadmap for 2027 and beyond includes expanding the eligible securities and asset servicing. For now settlement arrangements are up to Participants, but given the DTCC group’s critical role in securities settlement it is not surprising that it has plans in this area. Today netting via the NSCC typically reduces the settlement figure for conventional securities by around 98%, and the roadmap includes on-chain cash netting. The DTCC has previously told Ledger Insights it is exploring stablecoins and tokenized deposits for settlement. While not necessarily indicative, JPMorgan played a prominent role in the July live transactions and has said it plans to launch JPM Coin on Canton. Previous DTCC collateral simulations included Société Générale FORGE’s stablecoins and Fnality’s institutional settlement system. It remains to be seen whether use cases will bifurcate, with traditional finance attracted to 24/7 movement of collateral and crypto natives using DTC tokens to trade or to underpin wrapped tokens. Alpaca is among the launch participants and Ondo is named as a collaborator, which points toward wrapped tokens. Trading could happen via ATS venues or tokenized securities venues that are subject to the SEC’s innovation exemption. Canton may not be known as a major DeFi trading venue, but one of the first TSVs planning to launch, TSV LLC, is on the Canton Network. That said, it only plans to support issuer-sponsored tokens rather than third party tokens such as the DTCC’s.

title: JPM Coin Expands to Ethereum for Approved Institutional Clients - TradingView
content: TL;DR: J.P. The next evidence is transaction activity from approved institutions, additional supported use cases, integration with tokenised collateral and disclosures about outages and compliance controls. The latest development in JPM’s corner of the digital-asset market is worth examining beyond the headline. A 2026-10-19 announcement describes a concrete change, but the investment consequences will depend on how it works in practice. The original record is available in the original company statement; here is what it establishes, why the distinction matters and what remains unproven. J.P. Morgan said on October 19 that its JPM Coin deposit token, ticker JPMD, had been brought to Ethereum. The bank describes the service as available to eligible institutional clients, extending a token representing dollar deposits at J.P. Morgan to another public blockchain. It is not an open retail dollar coin anyone can mint or redeem freely. The important development is a major bank connecting its own deposit liabilities with blockchain-based institutional workflows rather than issuing an unrelated speculative crypto asset. A deposit token and an independently issued payment stablecoin can look similar in a wallet interface, but the legal claims and eligible users may be very different. JPM Coin represents money deposited with the bank, subject to its programme terms and access controls. J.P. Morgan has also used the Base network, another Ethereum-compatible environment. The Ethereum expansion therefore increases where approved institutions can move the token without necessarily changing who is permitted to hold it. The bank pointed to Ethereum’s liquidity and existing tokenised-asset activity as a reason for the integration. Large financial institutions are interested in placing cash next to securities on shared infrastructure so that trading, payments and collateral operations can be coordinated. Onchain cash legs may shorten operational handoffs, but legal settlement arrangements and counterparty exposure still matter. An Ethereum transfer being final at the protocol level is not a complete description of a regulated financial transaction. For cryptocurrency investors, the central point is to distinguish an announced milestone from an immediate change in asset value. The underlying development can strengthen a company’s product, legal position or operating capacity without determining what a token will trade for tomorrow. The linked source establishes what was disclosed; the valuation question requires a separate assessment of customers, costs, execution and market conditions. That gap between a confirmed fact and a forecast is where much of the investment risk sits. Running a bank-backed instrument on public networks introduces a deliberate mix of openness and permissioning. Validators and infrastructure may be widely distributed, yet the asset itself can restrict eligible holders and transfer paths. That hybrid design is often more realistic for regulated institutions than assuming all treasury assets must be freely transferable. It also complicates claims that public-chain adoption automatically means universal decentralised access for users. The next evidence is transaction activity from approved institutions, additional supported use cases, integration with tokenised collateral and disclosures about outages and compliance controls. The announcement confirms an Ethereum deployment but does not prove mainstream adoption by every banking customer. It shows how finance is experimenting with common blockchain infrastructure while preserving many of the boundaries and responsibilities of the conventional banking system. Market watchers should also avoid treating a company’s or regulator’s headline as a substitute for terms and conditions. Tokens, shares and regulated service agreements create different rights, even when they coexist in one wallet or platform. A reliable follow-up should ask which entity is responsible, what a holder can actually redeem or transfer, and whether the claimed advantages appear in live activity. Those questions are more informative than an unsupported price target or an assumption that adoption is inevitable. Primary source: original company statement (2026-10-19). title: J.P. Morgan Names Former Merrill Manager to Lead Southeast Market - AdvisorHub
content: Over a year after leaving thundering herd as part of a reorganization, former Merrill Lynch Private Wealth regional leader Linda A. Patel has returned to management at J.P. Morgan Advisors, the New York bank’s traditional brokerage unit. Linda A. Patel, who previously oversaw Merrill’s ultra-high net worth brokers in Texas, joined J.P. Morgan Advisors as head of its Southeast territory based in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, according to an announcement on Tuesday. Patel oversees around 80 advisors in Palm Beach Gardens, Palm Beach, Boca Raton, Miami and Atlanta, according to the announcement. She reports to J.P. Morgan Advisors Head Mollie Colavita and succeeds Janet Sweeney, a 40-year industry veteran who retired earlier this year. Sweeny had joined J.P. Morgan through its 2023 acquisition of First Republic Bank’s wealth unit. The appointment comes a little over a week after two of J.P. Morgan’s largest teams, who had generated $130 million in combined revenue from $18.6 billion in assets, left to launch RIA Latigo Peak Partners based in Palm Beach Gardens. “The Southeast continues to attract individuals, families and businesses with increasingly complex financial needs – creating significant opportunity for us to build on our strength in the region and grow alongside our clients,” Colavita said in a statement. Patel was one of two Merrill Private Wealth leaders who left in July 2025 as the firm consolidated six regions to four. She had led its Texas region since 2018 after overseeing offices in Thousand Oaks, California. Patel started her career at UBS’s PaineWebber predecessor in 1998 and joined Merrill through a predecessor later that year, according to BrokerCheck. She did not respond to a request for comment sent through social media. J.P. Morgan Advisors has around 600 advisors and remains a small fraction of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s wealth business. Colavita, a former senior executive at Merrill Private Wealth, took over the top job at J.P. Morgan Advisors in October 2025 following the retirement of Phil Sieg, who was once head of Merrill Private Wealth. A Merrill spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment. Despite shrinking advisor headcount, UBS’s net new assets rebounded to $16.7 billion in the third quarter.

For 55 years, On Lok has supported older adults across the Bay Area in accessing care and aging on their own terms. See how J.P. Morgan is backing On Lok’s next chapter with capital, expertise and a long-term relationship that goes beyond banking. In Cantonese, “On Lok” means happy, peaceful abode or home. The name carries both aspiration and promise, and, for more than five decades, the San Francisco nonprofit it describes has worked to make that promise real for thousands of older adults across the Bay Area. In 1971, a group of community members in San Francisco’s Chinatown North Beach neighborhood asked a deceptively simple question: Why should a person spend the final years of their life in a nursing home, far from the streets they walked, the food they loved and the language they spoke? Their answer: They shouldn’t. And that’s how On Lok was founded. For too many Americans, aging with dignity remains harder than it should be: Healthcare is fragmented, costs are rising and families navigate a maze of providers and social services. On Lok was built to meet that need. Problem: On Lok needed to open two new 23,000-square-foot centers in Union City and South San Jose simultaneously, while continuing to serve thousands of seniors across its existing programs, with complex multi-year financing needs that exceeded typical nonprofit banking. Solution: J.P. Morgan structured a $55 million direct purchase bond facility, drawing on its healthcare sector expertise to deliver creative, long-term financing. The firm complemented it with treasury management, healthcare payments technology and enterprise resource planning integration support to modernize On Lok’s operations at scale. Outcome: Both centers opened and have been fully operational since February 2026, expanding access to coordinated senior care for an estimated 800 additional seniors across the Bay Area. “It’s been 55 years now that On Lok has been part of this community,” said CEO Grace Li, who’s been with the organization for 25 years. “It came to be when members of our community recognized that the seniors in the Chinatown North Beach community really needed a way to receive care that was going to keep them close to their communities.” What emerged was the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly—known as PACE—a coordinated, community-based alternative to nursing home placement that integrates medical care, social services, nutrition, transportation and daily activities under one roof. As On Lok proved the model locally, its leaders wanted to test whether it could work beyond San Francisco. They took the concept to the federal government as a demonstration and established a unique way to finance the program through Medicare and Medicaid to deliver the full range of services seniors need to stay in their communities. With grant support, On Lok worked with six organizations in six states to teach the approach and show it could deliver quality care beyond a single city or population. That proof helped pave the way for a permanent funding framework within Medicare regulations. Today, PACE operates in 33 states and the District of Columbia, serving more than 100,000 people. With approximately $286 million in annual revenue and more than 1,200 employees, On Lok is also a significant economic anchor in the San Francisco Bay Area, contracting with local vendors and generating the institutional stability that keeps neighborhoods viable. “Organizations don’t shape policy and change payment reform by accident,” Li said. “Being a local nonprofit where people see our vans and know who On Lok is—they just know.” “People can still make their own choices. It’s not easy to age and On Lok has been thinking about what our community members need as they age for 55 years.” On Lok’s services span a continuum of aging: active seniors come to senior centers for exercise, art, computer labs and communal meals; those with more complex needs receive care management and help navigating insurance and housing; and for seniors whose chronic conditions make daily life genuinely difficult, the PACE program provides fully integrated medical and social support that keeps them in the community rather than in institutional care. “On Lok’s mission is the voice of aging,” said Nicole Torres, COO and a 24-year member of the organization. Torres began her career as a nurse—starting in pediatrics at Lucile Packard at Stanford—before shifting into older-adult care and joining On Lok as a home care nurse. “We are serving people who are yearning to age as they want to age. We are also serving communities that need us, who are vulnerable, who are unheard.” Marie, a pianist and PACE participant at the On Lok 30th Street Center, came to On Lok after breaking her femur during the pandemic. Today she plays piano for fellow participants several times a week. “I kept hoping I could play music for people again. The dream came true,” Marie said. She is also grateful for the healthcare support: “It’s a lifesaver for me.” Jeffrey, a 66-year-old former cable linesman and self-taught artist at the On Lok PACE South San Jose Center, has had his drawings celebrated by staff and shared with other participants. “The medical support here is impressive,” he said. “I thought I was at the end of my rope. It makes me feel like I’m still somebody. On Lok takes good care of me.” On Lok’s reach is deeply local: It employs physicians, nurses, social workers, therapists, drivers and nutritionists, and contracts with local small businesses and community providers. Its impact extends far beyond its walls, strengthening families, caregivers and the community institutions that make neighborhoods work. That’s the lens JPMorganChase applies through the American Dream Initiative: scaling proven local solutions by mobilizing capital, know-how and practical policy support alongside local organizations. The initiative was designed, in part, to finance local healthcare infrastructure that expands opportunity. For aging Americans, that opportunity means staying in your neighborhood, maintaining independence and receiving high-quality care without being uprooted from everything you know. “The work we do addresses healthcare, medical care and social supports for that senior and its impact goes beyond the senior,” Torres said. “It helps their community, the immediate caregivers, the friends, the daughters, the husband, the wife and then it helps the greater neighborhood.” Connect with our team to learn how J.P. Morgan can support your mission-driven organization in strengthening operations, accessing capital and scaling community impact. On Lok is not. We had to recognize who are experts in helping organizations think about how to scale.” J.P. Morgan provided a $55 million direct purchase bond facility to finance the acquisition and development of both sites, a transaction requiring careful multi-year planning and deep sector-specific expertise. “For this particular financing opportunity, we turned to J.P. Morgan and talked with them about ways that they could help support us,” Li said. “J.P. Morgan helped us with a huge historic endeavor,” Torres said. “After two years plus of blood, sweat and tears, those buildings are fully built out and we’ve been operational since February.” For Stu Bessieres, Relationship Executive at J.P. Morgan, the milestone is personal. “On Lok is a critical organization of San Francisco that represents our true San Franciscan identity. J.P. Morgan was integral in providing the capital necessary for On Lok to expand in both their Union City and South San Jose locations. I saw the buses driving around growing up. Now I get to truly be a part of its success.” J.P. Morgan is supporting On Lok’s migration to an enterprise resource planning (ERP) platform, transitioning reconciliation and payment origination from manual to fully automated processes. The organization is now serving the children and grandchildren of the first seniors it cared for in 1971. That generational continuity is both a measure of past success and a mandate for what comes next. “We’re already serving generations of families,” Li said. “There are grandkids who always would come and know On Lok because they visited their grandparent here or their parent here.” Torres looks ahead with clarity. “The next 55 years look bright. title: JPMorgan Chase Says That Bitcoin Will Outperform Stocks, Bonds, and Gold Over the Next 10 Years. Here's Why It Might Be Right - The Motley Fool
content: The banking giant is still pretty skeptical about Bitcoin. Per a new report, the asset management arm of JPMorgan Chase (JPM +1.26%) has a base case in which Bitcoin (BTC -3.28%) beats domestic stocks, bonds, and even gold during the next 10 years. It expects the crypto to return 10% annually during that period, versus 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 5.6% for broad U.S. bonds, and 5.5% for gold. It's the first time the report has put a range on Bitcoin's returns, and it comes with a handful of heavy caveats. Although the figures it calculated are unlikely to prove true in 2036, the drivers for those results are hard to argue against, and it's my view that JPMorgan Chase is directionally correct. Here's why. The JPMorgan Chase report is largely about the investing implications of the macroeconomic conditions facing the world during the coming years, touching on everything from inflation to global warming and, of course, Bitcoin. It expects artificial-intelligence-driven productivity gains to push the U.S. economy's real growth rate to 2.1% annually, with inflation averaging 2.4% in the same period. It also raised its expected annual return for large companies, such as those in the S&P 500 index, from 6.7% to 7.5%, citing strong profit margins. But it contends that Bitcoin will be buoyed by three different factors that will offer better performance than this. The most important driver, with a 65% weight in the calculation, is Bitcoin's slowing supply growth relative to global money growth. The second-most-important factor, with a weight of 30%, is Bitcoin's inclusion in portfolios alongside allocations to other scarce store-of-value assets, such as gold. The last driver is the weakest: the coin's increasing network activity. The bank's estimated growth rate for its base case implies that Bitcoin would be priced at about $211,130 by 2036. Its bear case, which calls for an 11.2% annual loss, implies a price of about $24,817, roughly 70% below its $81,300 level as of Oct. 26. The bull case would see it grow by 16.6% annually. But no matter which of those scenarios plays out, the bank expects the coin's volatility to be 55%, based on historical data. Overall, JPMorgan Chase's projections for Bitcoin's price growth are on the bearish side compared to Bitcoin's history, but they look reasonable. The coin has a 10-year compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 63%. The supply model is difficult to dispute; Bitcoin's next halving, when the number of new coins miners earn per block is halved, is expected sometime in April 2028. The U.S. M2, one gauge of the broad money supply, grew by 5.7% in the year through August 2026. The bank doubts that a currency-debasement scare will spark a rush into crypto, but its model doe assumes a modest shift. Its projected inflation during the next decade is significantly lower than September 2026's 3.7% annual pace, which means that if inflation remains elevated, the importance of Bitcoin as a potential hedge against it could drive its performance toward the bull case. Still, the bank calls the coin "a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing." It says volatility has declined, but unstable correlations make Bitcoin premature as a diversifier. Though JPMorgan Chase still doesn't recommend buying Bitcoin, it probably makes sense to own at least a little to gain exposure to its upside in the bank's base case, and perhaps a bit more upside if the bull case plays out. It stands to be a bountiful holiday quarter for some of the world's biggest banks, courtesy of the gift-giving team at Anthropic (ANTH.PVT). Using the SpaceX IPO fee rate, allocations, and a range of potential proceeds, EvercoreISI analyst Glenn Schorr estimates Anthropic's offering could generate a roughly $562 million equity capital markets (ECM) fee pool. That would equal about 1% of fourth-quarter consensus EPS across the banks he covers. In Schorr's base case, co-lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley would each haul in $112 million in fees. Bank of America, Citigroup, and JPMorgan would each rake in $84 million. A total of 22 banks appear on Anthropic's IPO tombstone, an advertisement recognizing the investment banks and other financial firms helping take the company public. "A successful listing could also encourage more AI companies to test the public markets, accelerate broader IPO momentum, and reinforce the view that the AI trade still has room to run," Schorr added. Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus shows. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead. Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion. Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November. "I think this needs to be valued appropriately," Manhattan Ventures co-founder Jare Carmel said on Sozzi Unleashed. Manhattan Venture Partners is an investor in Anthropic. "I think the biggest problem that we've seen in the IPO markets over the last few years are sort of valuations that have been offsides. And this needs to be valued to sell the IPO buyer, whether that's institutional or retail. They seem to hop around, especially when they're not getting the pop that they need. And I can fully understand why a company like Anthropic wouldn't would want to value themselves fairly as opposed to, let's say, undervalued. But the reality is you need to have shareholders for the long term."
